import argparse
from estate.core.ledger import create_change
from estate.core.residents import register_resident
from estate.core.registry import load_registry
from estate.core.paths import ESTATE_ROOT, LEDGER_PATH, DEVLOG_PATH

def cmd_change(args):
    ec_id = create_change(args.title, args.summary, args.status, args.classification)
    print(f"Created {ec_id}: {args.title}")

def cmd_resident(args):
    res_id, ec_id = register_resident(
        name=args.name,
        department=args.department,
        office=args.office,
        role=args.role,
        classification=args.classification
    )
    print(f"Created {res_id}")
    print(f"Logged {ec_id}")

def cmd_status(args):
    print("Estate Core Status")
    print(f"Root: {ESTATE_ROOT}")
    print(f"Ledger: {LEDGER_PATH.exists()} - {LEDGER_PATH}")
    print(f"Devlog: {DEVLOG_PATH.exists()} - {DEVLOG_PATH}")
    residents = load_registry("residents")
    print(f"Registered residents: {len(residents)}")

def cmd_list_residents(args):
    residents = load_registry("residents")
    if not residents:
        print("No residents registered.")
        return
    for item in residents:
        print(f'{item["id"]} | {item["name"]} | {item["department"]} | {item["office"]}')

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="estate", description="Estate Core CLI")
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command")

    p = sub.add_parser("change")
    p.add_argument("--title", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--summary", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--status", default="Draft")
    p.add_argument("--classification", default="Estate Internal")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_change)

    p = sub.add_parser("resident")
    p.add_argument("--name", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--department", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--office", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--role", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--classification", default="Estate Internal")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_resident)

    p = sub.add_parser("status")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_status)

    p = sub.add_parser("list-residents")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_list_residents)

    args = parser.parse_args()
    if not hasattr(args, "func"):
        parser.print_help()
        return
    args.func(args)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import json
from pathlib import Path
from estate.core.paths import REGISTRY_DIR, OBJECTS_DIR
from estate.core.time import now

def ensure_dirs():
    REGISTRY_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    OBJECTS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

def registry_path(object_type):
    ensure_dirs()
    return REGISTRY_DIR / f"{object_type}.json"

def load_registry(object_type):
    path = registry_path(object_type)
    if not path.exists():
        return []
    return json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

def save_registry(object_type, items):
    path = registry_path(object_type)
    path.write_text(json.dumps(items, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

def add_registry_object(object_type, obj):
    items = load_registry(object_type)
    obj["registered_at"] = obj.get("registered_at") or now()
    items.append(obj)
    save_registry(object_type, items)

def write_object_file(object_id, obj):
    ensure_dirs()
    path = OBJECTS_DIR / f"{object_id}.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps(obj, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    return path

from estate.core.paths import LEDGER_PATH, DEVLOG_PATH
from estate.core.ids import next_number, make_id
from estate.core.time import now

def _read(path):
    return path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") if path.exists() else ""

def _append(path, text):
    with path.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text)

def next_ec_id():
    text = _read(LEDGER_PATH)
    return make_id("EC", next_number("EC", text))

def create_change(title, summary, status="Draft", classification="Estate Internal", location=r"A:\theestate"):
    ec_id = next_ec_id()
    timestamp = now()

    ledger_entry = f"""

## {ec_id} - {title}

Timestamp: {timestamp}
Location: {location}
Status: {status}
Classification: {classification}

Summary:
{summary}
"""
    _append(LEDGER_PATH, ledger_entry)

    devlog_entry = f"""

## {timestamp}

{ec_id} - {title}

{summary}
"""
    _append(DEVLOG_PATH, devlog_entry)

    return ec_id

from estate.core.paths import RESIDENTS_DIR
from estate.core.ids import next_number, make_id
from estate.core.registry import load_registry, add_registry_object, write_object_file
from estate.core.ledger import create_change
from estate.core.time import now

def next_resident_id():
    items = load_registry("residents")
    text = "\n".join([item.get("id", "") for item in items])
    return make_id("RES", next_number("RES", text))

def register_resident(name, department, office, role, classification="Estate Internal"):
    RESIDENTS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    resident_id = next_resident_id()
    safe = name.lower().replace(" ", "_")

    obj = {
        "id": resident_id,
        "type": "resident",
        "name": name,
        "department": department,
        "office": office,
        "status": "Active",
        "classification": classification,
        "created": now(),
        "role": role,
        "canonical": f"estate://residents/{resident_id.lower()}",
        "palace": f"Estate / Residents / {name}"
    }

    add_registry_object("residents", obj)
    write_object_file(resident_id, obj)

    markdown = f"""# {name}

ID: {resident_id}
Name: {name}
Department: {department}
Office: {office}
Status: Active
Classification: {classification}
Created: {obj["created"]}
Canonical: {obj["canonical"]}
Palace: {obj["palace"]}

## Role

{role}

## Notes

Registered by Estate Core.
"""
    (RESIDENTS_DIR / f"{safe}.md").write_text(markdown, encoding="utf-8")

    ec_id = create_change(
        title=f"Registered Resident {name}",
        summary=f"Created resident record {resident_id} for {name}, serving as {office} in {department}."
    )

    return resident_id, ec_id

import argparse
from estate.core.ledger import create_change
from estate.core.residents import register_resident
from estate.core.registry import load_registry
from estate.core.paths import ESTATE_ROOT, LEDGER_PATH, DEVLOG_PATH

def cmd_change(args):
    ec_id = create_change(args.title, args.summary, args.status, args.classification)
    print(f"Created {ec_id}: {args.title}")

def cmd_resident(args):
    res_id, ec_id = register_resident(
        name=args.name,
        department=args.department,
        office=args.office,
        role=args.role,
        classification=args.classification
    )
    print(f"Created {res_id}")
    print(f"Logged {ec_id}")

def cmd_status(args):
    print("Estate Core Status")
    print(f"Root: {ESTATE_ROOT}")
    print(f"Ledger: {LEDGER_PATH.exists()} - {LEDGER_PATH}")
    print(f"Devlog: {DEVLOG_PATH.exists()} - {DEVLOG_PATH}")
    residents = load_registry("residents")
    print(f"Registered residents: {len(residents)}")

def cmd_list_residents(args):
    residents = load_registry("residents")
    if not residents:
        print("No residents registered.")
        return
    for item in residents:
        print(f'{item["id"]} | {item["name"]} | {item["department"]} | {item["office"]}')

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="estate", description="Estate Core CLI")
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command")

    p = sub.add_parser("change")
    p.add_argument("--title", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--summary", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--status", default="Draft")
    p.add_argument("--classification", default="Estate Internal")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_change)

    p = sub.add_parser("resident")
    p.add_argument("--name", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--department", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--office", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--role", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--classification", default="Estate Internal")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_resident)

    p = sub.add_parser("status")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_status)

    p = sub.add_parser("list-residents")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_list_residents)

    args = parser.parse_args()
    if not hasattr(args, "func"):
        parser.print_help()
        return
    args.func(args)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"@ | Set-Content src\estate\core\time.py

@"
import re

def next_number(prefix, text):
    pattern = re.compile(rf"{prefix}-(\d+)")
    nums = [int(m.group(1)) for m in pattern.finditer(text)]
    return max(nums) + 1 if nums else 1

def make_id(prefix, number):
    return f"{prefix}-{number:06d}"

import json
from pathlib import Path
from estate.core.paths import REGISTRY_DIR, OBJECTS_DIR
from estate.core.time import now

def ensure_dirs():
    REGISTRY_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    OBJECTS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

def registry_path(object_type):
    ensure_dirs()
    return REGISTRY_DIR / f"{object_type}.json"

def load_registry(object_type):
    path = registry_path(object_type)
    if not path.exists():
        return []
    return json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

def save_registry(object_type, items):
    path = registry_path(object_type)
    path.write_text(json.dumps(items, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

def add_registry_object(object_type, obj):
    items = load_registry(object_type)
    obj["registered_at"] = obj.get("registered_at") or now()
    items.append(obj)
    save_registry(object_type, items)

def write_object_file(object_id, obj):
    ensure_dirs()
    path = OBJECTS_DIR / f"{object_id}.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps(obj, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    return path

from estate.core.paths import LEDGER_PATH, DEVLOG_PATH
from estate.core.ids import next_number, make_id
from estate.core.time import now

def _read(path):
    return path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") if path.exists() else ""

def _append(path, text):
    with path.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text)

def next_ec_id():
    text = _read(LEDGER_PATH)
    return make_id("EC", next_number("EC", text))

def create_change(title, summary, status="Draft", classification="Estate Internal", location=r"A:\theestate"):
    ec_id = next_ec_id()
    timestamp = now()

    ledger_entry = f"""

## {ec_id} - {title}

Timestamp: {timestamp}
Location: {location}
Status: {status}
Classification: {classification}

Summary:
{summary}
"""
    _append(LEDGER_PATH, ledger_entry)

    devlog_entry = f"""

## {timestamp}

{ec_id} - {title}

{summary}
"""
    _append(DEVLOG_PATH, devlog_entry)

    return ec_id

from estate.core.paths import RESIDENTS_DIR
from estate.core.ids import next_number, make_id
from estate.core.registry import load_registry, add_registry_object, write_object_file
from estate.core.ledger import create_change
from estate.core.time import now

def next_resident_id():
    items = load_registry("residents")
    text = "\n".join([item.get("id", "") for item in items])
    return make_id("RES", next_number("RES", text))

def register_resident(name, department, office, role, classification="Estate Internal"):
    RESIDENTS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    resident_id = next_resident_id()
    safe = name.lower().replace(" ", "_")

    obj = {
        "id": resident_id,
        "type": "resident",
        "name": name,
        "department": department,
        "office": office,
        "status": "Active",
        "classification": classification,
        "created": now(),
        "role": role,
        "canonical": f"estate://residents/{resident_id.lower()}",
        "palace": f"Estate / Residents / {name}"
    }

    add_registry_object("residents", obj)
    write_object_file(resident_id, obj)

    markdown = f"""# {name}

ID: {resident_id}
Name: {name}
Department: {department}
Office: {office}
Status: Active
Classification: {classification}
Created: {obj["created"]}
Canonical: {obj["canonical"]}
Palace: {obj["palace"]}

## Role

{role}

## Notes

Registered by Estate Core.
"""
    (RESIDENTS_DIR / f"{safe}.md").write_text(markdown, encoding="utf-8")

    ec_id = create_change(
        title=f"Registered Resident {name}",
        summary=f"Created resident record {resident_id} for {name}, serving as {office} in {department}."
    )

    return resident_id, ec_id

import argparse
from estate.core.ledger import create_change
from estate.core.residents import register_resident
from estate.core.registry import load_registry
from estate.core.paths import ESTATE_ROOT, LEDGER_PATH, DEVLOG_PATH

def cmd_change(args):
    ec_id = create_change(args.title, args.summary, args.status, args.classification)
    print(f"Created {ec_id}: {args.title}")

def cmd_resident(args):
    res_id, ec_id = register_resident(
        name=args.name,
        department=args.department,
        office=args.office,
        role=args.role,
        classification=args.classification
    )
    print(f"Created {res_id}")
    print(f"Logged {ec_id}")

def cmd_status(args):
    print("Estate Core Status")
    print(f"Root: {ESTATE_ROOT}")
    print(f"Ledger: {LEDGER_PATH.exists()} - {LEDGER_PATH}")
    print(f"Devlog: {DEVLOG_PATH.exists()} - {DEVLOG_PATH}")
    residents = load_registry("residents")
    print(f"Registered residents: {len(residents)}")

def cmd_list_residents(args):
    residents = load_registry("residents")
    if not residents:
        print("No residents registered.")
        return
    for item in residents:
        print(f'{item["id"]} | {item["name"]} | {item["department"]} | {item["office"]}')

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="estate", description="Estate Core CLI")
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command")

    p = sub.add_parser("change")
    p.add_argument("--title", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--summary", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--status", default="Draft")
    p.add_argument("--classification", default="Estate Internal")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_change)

    p = sub.add_parser("resident")
    p.add_argument("--name", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--department", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--office", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--role", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--classification", default="Estate Internal")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_resident)

    p = sub.add_parser("status")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_status)

    p = sub.add_parser("list-residents")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_list_residents)

    args = parser.parse_args()
    if not hasattr(args, "func"):
        parser.print_help()
        return
    args.func(args)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

from datetime import datetime

def now():
    return datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
"@ | Set-Content src\estate\core\time.py

@"
import re

def next_number(prefix, text):
    pattern = re.compile(rf"{prefix}-(\d+)")
    nums = [int(m.group(1)) for m in pattern.finditer(text)]
    return max(nums) + 1 if nums else 1

def make_id(prefix, number):
    return f"{prefix}-{number:06d}"
"@ | Set-Content src\estate\core\ids.py

@"
import json
from pathlib import Path
from estate.core.paths import REGISTRY_DIR, OBJECTS_DIR
from estate.core.time import now

def ensure_dirs():
    REGISTRY_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    OBJECTS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

def registry_path(object_type):
    ensure_dirs()
    return REGISTRY_DIR / f"{object_type}.json"

def load_registry(object_type):
    path = registry_path(object_type)
    if not path.exists():
        return []
    return json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

def save_registry(object_type, items):
    path = registry_path(object_type)
    path.write_text(json.dumps(items, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

def add_registry_object(object_type, obj):
    items = load_registry(object_type)
    obj["registered_at"] = obj.get("registered_at") or now()
    items.append(obj)
    save_registry(object_type, items)

def write_object_file(object_id, obj):
    ensure_dirs()
    path = OBJECTS_DIR / f"{object_id}.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps(obj, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    return path
"@ | Set-Content src\estate\core\registry.py

from estate.core.paths import LEDGER_PATH, DEVLOG_PATH
from estate.core.ids import next_number, make_id
from estate.core.time import now

def _read(path):
    return path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") if path.exists() else ""

def _append(path, text):
    with path.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text)

def next_ec_id():
    text = _read(LEDGER_PATH)
    return make_id("EC", next_number("EC", text))

def create_change(title, summary, status="Draft", classification="Estate Internal", location=r"A:\theestate"):
    ec_id = next_ec_id()
    timestamp = now()

    ledger_entry = f"""

## {ec_id} - {title}

Timestamp: {timestamp}
Location: {location}
Status: {status}
Classification: {classification}

Summary:
{summary}
"""
    _append(LEDGER_PATH, ledger_entry)

    devlog_entry = f"""

## {timestamp}

{ec_id} - {title}

{summary}
"""
    _append(DEVLOG_PATH, devlog_entry)

    return ec_id

from estate.core.paths import RESIDENTS_DIR
from estate.core.ids import next_number, make_id
from estate.core.registry import load_registry, add_registry_object, write_object_file
from estate.core.ledger import create_change
from estate.core.time import now

def next_resident_id():
    items = load_registry("residents")
    text = "\n".join([item.get("id", "") for item in items])
    return make_id("RES", next_number("RES", text))

def register_resident(name, department, office, role, classification="Estate Internal"):
    RESIDENTS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    resident_id = next_resident_id()
    safe = name.lower().replace(" ", "_")

    obj = {
        "id": resident_id,
        "type": "resident",
        "name": name,
        "department": department,
        "office": office,
        "status": "Active",
        "classification": classification,
        "created": now(),
        "role": role,
        "canonical": f"estate://residents/{resident_id.lower()}",
        "palace": f"Estate / Residents / {name}"
    }

    add_registry_object("residents", obj)
    write_object_file(resident_id, obj)

    markdown = f"""# {name}

ID: {resident_id}
Name: {name}
Department: {department}
Office: {office}
Status: Active
Classification: {classification}
Created: {obj["created"]}
Canonical: {obj["canonical"]}
Palace: {obj["palace"]}

## Role

{role}

## Notes

Registered by Estate Core.
"""
    (RESIDENTS_DIR / f"{safe}.md").write_text(markdown, encoding="utf-8")

    ec_id = create_change(
        title=f"Registered Resident {name}",
        summary=f"Created resident record {resident_id} for {name}, serving as {office} in {department}."
    )

    return resident_id, ec_id
"@ | Set-Content src\estate\core\residents.py

import argparse
from estate.core.ledger import create_change
from estate.core.residents import register_resident
from estate.core.registry import load_registry
from estate.core.paths import ESTATE_ROOT, LEDGER_PATH, DEVLOG_PATH

def cmd_change(args):
    ec_id = create_change(args.title, args.summary, args.status, args.classification)
    print(f"Created {ec_id}: {args.title}")

def cmd_resident(args):
    res_id, ec_id = register_resident(
        name=args.name,
        department=args.department,
        office=args.office,
        role=args.role,
        classification=args.classification
    )
    print(f"Created {res_id}")
    print(f"Logged {ec_id}")

def cmd_status(args):
    print("Estate Core Status")
    print(f"Root: {ESTATE_ROOT}")
    print(f"Ledger: {LEDGER_PATH.exists()} - {LEDGER_PATH}")
    print(f"Devlog: {DEVLOG_PATH.exists()} - {DEVLOG_PATH}")
    residents = load_registry("residents")
    print(f"Registered residents: {len(residents)}")

def cmd_list_residents(args):
    residents = load_registry("residents")
    if not residents:
        print("No residents registered.")
        return
    for item in residents:
        print(f'{item["id"]} | {item["name"]} | {item["department"]} | {item["office"]}')

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="estate", description="Estate Core CLI")
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command")

    p = sub.add_parser("change")
    p.add_argument("--title", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--summary", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--status", default="Draft")
    p.add_argument("--classification", default="Estate Internal")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_change)

    p = sub.add_parser("resident")
    p.add_argument("--name", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--department", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--office", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--role", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--classification", default="Estate Internal")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_resident)

    p = sub.add_parser("status")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_status)

    p = sub.add_parser("list-residents")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_list_residents)

    args = parser.parse_args()
    if not hasattr(args, "func"):
        parser.print_help()
        return
    args.func(args)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

from datetime import datetime

def now():
    return datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
"@ | Set-Content src\estate\core\time.py

@"
import re

def next_number(prefix, text):
    pattern = re.compile(rf"{prefix}-(\d+)")
    nums = [int(m.group(1)) for m in pattern.finditer(text)]
    return max(nums) + 1 if nums else 1

def make_id(prefix, number):
    return f"{prefix}-{number:06d}"
"@ | Set-Content src\estate\core\ids.py

@"
import json
from pathlib import Path
from estate.core.paths import REGISTRY_DIR, OBJECTS_DIR
from estate.core.time import now

def ensure_dirs():
    REGISTRY_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    OBJECTS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

def registry_path(object_type):
    ensure_dirs()
    return REGISTRY_DIR / f"{object_type}.json"

def load_registry(object_type):
    path = registry_path(object_type)
    if not path.exists():
        return []
    return json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

def save_registry(object_type, items):
    path = registry_path(object_type)
    path.write_text(json.dumps(items, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

def add_registry_object(object_type, obj):
    items = load_registry(object_type)
    obj["registered_at"] = obj.get("registered_at") or now()
    items.append(obj)
    save_registry(object_type, items)

def write_object_file(object_id, obj):
    ensure_dirs()
    path = OBJECTS_DIR / f"{object_id}.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps(obj, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    return path

from estate.core.paths import LEDGER_PATH, DEVLOG_PATH
from estate.core.ids import next_number, make_id
from estate.core.time import now

def _read(path):
    return path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") if path.exists() else ""

def _append(path, text):
    with path.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text)

def next_ec_id():
    text = _read(LEDGER_PATH)
    return make_id("EC", next_number("EC", text))

def create_change(title, summary, status="Draft", classification="Estate Internal", location=r"A:\theestate"):
    ec_id = next_ec_id()
    timestamp = now()

    ledger_entry = f"""

## {ec_id} - {title}

Timestamp: {timestamp}
Location: {location}
Status: {status}
Classification: {classification}

Summary:
{summary}
"""
    _append(LEDGER_PATH, ledger_entry)

    devlog_entry = f"""

## {timestamp}

{ec_id} - {title}

{summary}
"""
    _append(DEVLOG_PATH, devlog_entry)

    return ec_id

from estate.core.paths import RESIDENTS_DIR
from estate.core.ids import next_number, make_id
from estate.core.registry import load_registry, add_registry_object, write_object_file
from estate.core.ledger import create_change
from estate.core.time import now

def next_resident_id():
    items = load_registry("residents")
    text = "\n".join([item.get("id", "") for item in items])
    return make_id("RES", next_number("RES", text))

def register_resident(name, department, office, role, classification="Estate Internal"):
    RESIDENTS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    resident_id = next_resident_id()
    safe = name.lower().replace(" ", "_")

    obj = {
        "id": resident_id,
        "type": "resident",
        "name": name,
        "department": department,
        "office": office,
        "status": "Active",
        "classification": classification,
        "created": now(),
        "role": role,
        "canonical": f"estate://residents/{resident_id.lower()}",
        "palace": f"Estate / Residents / {name}"
    }

    add_registry_object("residents", obj)
    write_object_file(resident_id, obj)

    markdown = f"""# {name}

ID: {resident_id}
Name: {name}
Department: {department}
Office: {office}
Status: Active
Classification: {classification}
Created: {obj["created"]}
Canonical: {obj["canonical"]}
Palace: {obj["palace"]}

## Role

{role}

## Notes

Registered by Estate Core.
"""
    (RESIDENTS_DIR / f"{safe}.md").write_text(markdown, encoding="utf-8")

    ec_id = create_change(
        title=f"Registered Resident {name}",
        summary=f"Created resident record {resident_id} for {name}, serving as {office} in {department}."
    )

    return resident_id, ec_id

import argparse
from estate.core.ledger import create_change
from estate.core.residents import register_resident
from estate.core.registry import load_registry
from estate.core.paths import ESTATE_ROOT, LEDGER_PATH, DEVLOG_PATH

def cmd_change(args):
    ec_id = create_change(args.title, args.summary, args.status, args.classification)
    print(f"Created {ec_id}: {args.title}")

def cmd_resident(args):
    res_id, ec_id = register_resident(
        name=args.name,
        department=args.department,
        office=args.office,
        role=args.role,
        classification=args.classification
    )
    print(f"Created {res_id}")
    print(f"Logged {ec_id}")

def cmd_status(args):
    print("Estate Core Status")
    print(f"Root: {ESTATE_ROOT}")
    print(f"Ledger: {LEDGER_PATH.exists()} - {LEDGER_PATH}")
    print(f"Devlog: {DEVLOG_PATH.exists()} - {DEVLOG_PATH}")
    residents = load_registry("residents")
    print(f"Registered residents: {len(residents)}")

def cmd_list_residents(args):
    residents = load_registry("residents")
    if not residents:
        print("No residents registered.")
        return
    for item in residents:
        print(f'{item["id"]} | {item["name"]} | {item["department"]} | {item["office"]}')

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="estate", description="Estate Core CLI")
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command")

    p = sub.add_parser("change")
    p.add_argument("--title", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--summary", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--status", default="Draft")
    p.add_argument("--classification", default="Estate Internal")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_change)

    p = sub.add_parser("resident")
    p.add_argument("--name", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--department", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--office", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--role", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--classification", default="Estate Internal")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_resident)

    p = sub.add_parser("status")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_status)

    p = sub.add_parser("list-residents")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_list_residents)

    args = parser.parse_args()
    if not hasattr(args, "func"):
        parser.print_help()
        return
    args.func(args)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

from datetime import datetime

def now():
    return datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
"@ | Set-Content src\estate\core\time.py

@"
import re

def next_number(prefix, text):
    pattern = re.compile(rf"{prefix}-(\d+)")
    nums = [int(m.group(1)) for m in pattern.finditer(text)]
    return max(nums) + 1 if nums else 1

def make_id(prefix, number):
    return f"{prefix}-{number:06d}"
"@ | Set-Content src\estate\core\ids.py

@"
import json
from pathlib import Path
from estate.core.paths import REGISTRY_DIR, OBJECTS_DIR
from estate.core.time import now

def ensure_dirs():
    REGISTRY_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    OBJECTS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

def registry_path(object_type):
    ensure_dirs()
    return REGISTRY_DIR / f"{object_type}.json"

def load_registry(object_type):
    path = registry_path(object_type)
    if not path.exists():
        return []
    return json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

def save_registry(object_type, items):
    path = registry_path(object_type)
    path.write_text(json.dumps(items, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")

def add_registry_object(object_type, obj):
    items = load_registry(object_type)
    obj["registered_at"] = obj.get("registered_at") or now()
    items.append(obj)
    save_registry(object_type, items)

def write_object_file(object_id, obj):
    ensure_dirs()
    path = OBJECTS_DIR / f"{object_id}.json"
    path.write_text(json.dumps(obj, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    return path
"@ | Set-Content src\estate\core\registry.py

from estate.core.paths import LEDGER_PATH, DEVLOG_PATH
from estate.core.ids import next_number, make_id
from estate.core.time import now

def _read(path):
    return path.read_text(encoding="utf-8") if path.exists() else ""

def _append(path, text):
    with path.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text)

def next_ec_id():
    text = _read(LEDGER_PATH)
    return make_id("EC", next_number("EC", text))

def create_change(title, summary, status="Draft", classification="Estate Internal", location=r"A:\theestate"):
    ec_id = next_ec_id()
    timestamp = now()

    ledger_entry = f"""

## {ec_id} - {title}

Timestamp: {timestamp}
Location: {location}
Status: {status}
Classification: {classification}

Summary:
{summary}
"""
    _append(LEDGER_PATH, ledger_entry)

    devlog_entry = f"""

## {timestamp}

{ec_id} - {title}

{summary}
"""
    _append(DEVLOG_PATH, devlog_entry)

    return ec_id
"@ | Set-Content src\estate\core\ledger.py

from estate.core.paths import RESIDENTS_DIR
from estate.core.ids import next_number, make_id
from estate.core.registry import load_registry, add_registry_object, write_object_file
from estate.core.ledger import create_change
from estate.core.time import now

def next_resident_id():
    items = load_registry("residents")
    text = "\n".join([item.get("id", "") for item in items])
    return make_id("RES", next_number("RES", text))

def register_resident(name, department, office, role, classification="Estate Internal"):
    RESIDENTS_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    resident_id = next_resident_id()
    safe = name.lower().replace(" ", "_")

    obj = {
        "id": resident_id,
        "type": "resident",
        "name": name,
        "department": department,
        "office": office,
        "status": "Active",
        "classification": classification,
        "created": now(),
        "role": role,
        "canonical": f"estate://residents/{resident_id.lower()}",
        "palace": f"Estate / Residents / {name}"
    }

    add_registry_object("residents", obj)
    write_object_file(resident_id, obj)

    markdown = f"""# {name}

ID: {resident_id}
Name: {name}
Department: {department}
Office: {office}
Status: Active
Classification: {classification}
Created: {obj["created"]}
Canonical: {obj["canonical"]}
Palace: {obj["palace"]}

## Role

{role}

## Notes

Registered by Estate Core.
"""
    (RESIDENTS_DIR / f"{safe}.md").write_text(markdown, encoding="utf-8")

    ec_id = create_change(
        title=f"Registered Resident {name}",
        summary=f"Created resident record {resident_id} for {name}, serving as {office} in {department}."
    )

    return resident_id, ec_id
"@ | Set-Content src\estate\core\residents.py

@"
import argparse
from estate.core.ledger import create_change
from estate.core.residents import register_resident
from estate.core.registry import load_registry
from estate.core.paths import ESTATE_ROOT, LEDGER_PATH, DEVLOG_PATH

def cmd_change(args):
    ec_id = create_change(args.title, args.summary, args.status, args.classification)
    print(f"Created {ec_id}: {args.title}")

def cmd_resident(args):
    res_id, ec_id = register_resident(
        name=args.name,
        department=args.department,
        office=args.office,
        role=args.role,
        classification=args.classification
    )
    print(f"Created {res_id}")
    print(f"Logged {ec_id}")

def cmd_status(args):
    print("Estate Core Status")
    print(f"Root: {ESTATE_ROOT}")
    print(f"Ledger: {LEDGER_PATH.exists()} - {LEDGER_PATH}")
    print(f"Devlog: {DEVLOG_PATH.exists()} - {DEVLOG_PATH}")
    residents = load_registry("residents")
    print(f"Registered residents: {len(residents)}")

def cmd_list_residents(args):
    residents = load_registry("residents")
    if not residents:
        print("No residents registered.")
        return
    for item in residents:
        print(f'{item["id"]} | {item["name"]} | {item["department"]} | {item["office"]}')

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="estate", description="Estate Core CLI")
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command")

    p = sub.add_parser("change")
    p.add_argument("--title", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--summary", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--status", default="Draft")
    p.add_argument("--classification", default="Estate Internal")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_change)

    p = sub.add_parser("resident")
    p.add_argument("--name", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--department", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--office", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--role", required=True)
    p.add_argument("--classification", default="Estate Internal")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_resident)

    p = sub.add_parser("status")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_status)

    p = sub.add_parser("list-residents")
    p.set_defaults(func=cmd_list_residents)

    args = parser.parse_args()
    if not hasattr(args, "func"):
        parser.print_help()
        return
    args.func(args)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
"@ | Set-Content src\estate\cli\main.py

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

Edit

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

I'd call it something like:

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

The goal would be to recover everything we've already designed before adding more.

That includes:

Resident biographies.

Office charters.

Personality profiles.

Speech style.

Catchphrases.

Authority boundaries.

Security clearances.

Decision authority.

Relationships between residents.

Trust model.

Architectural decisions.

Why decisions were made, not just what was built.

This is different from the Constitution. The Constitution should remain relatively small and stable. What we're talking about is a Project Brain or Institutional Design Record that preserves the reasoning behind the Estate.

I also think we should build a recovery process.

Rather than dumping one enormous summary, I'd organize it into volumes, for example:

Volume 1 — Vision and Philosophy

Volume 2 — Institutional Structure

Volume 3 — Residents and Offices

Volume 4 — Technical Architecture

Volume 5 — Discovery and Audit Evolution

Volume 6 — AI Infrastructure

Volume 7 — Historical Timeline

Volume 8 — Open Questions and Deferred Ideas

Each volume would be traceable back to the conversations that established it.

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

I'd call it something like:

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

The goal would be to recover everything we've already designed before adding more.

That includes:

Resident biographies.

Office charters.

Personality profiles.

Speech style.

Catchphrases.

Authority boundaries.

Security clearances.

Decision authority.

Relationships between residents.

Trust model.

Architectural decisions.

Why decisions were made, not just what was built.

This is different from the Constitution. The Constitution should remain relatively small and stable. What we're talking about is a Project Brain or Institutional Design Record that preserves the reasoning behind the Estate.

I also think we should build a recovery process.

Rather than dumping one enormous summary, I'd organize it into volumes, for example:

Volume 1 — Vision and Philosophy

Volume 2 — Institutional Structure

Volume 3 — Residents and Offices

Volume 4 — Technical Architecture

Volume 5 — Discovery and Audit Evolution

Volume 6 — AI Infrastructure

Volume 7 — Historical Timeline

Volume 8 — Open Questions and Deferred Ideas

Each volume would be traceable back to the conversations that established it.

About repasting the conversation

If you decide to do that, I think we can do it in a disciplined way.

Instead of trying to summarize from memory, we'll treat the conversation as primary source material. We'll extract facts, decisions, and rationale, assign confidence and provenance where appropriate, and build the Estate's institutional knowledge from that source. That approach fits perfectly with the principles we've been establishing.

That will give Alfred—and any future resident—a reliable institutional memory to build on rather than relying on the limits of a single conversation.

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

I'd call it something like:

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

The goal would be to recover everything we've already designed before adding more.

That includes:

Resident biographies.

Office charters.

Personality profiles.

Speech style.

Catchphrases.

Authority boundaries.

Security clearances.

Decision authority.

Relationships between residents.

Trust model.

Architectural decisions.

Why decisions were made, not just what was built.

This is different from the Constitution. The Constitution should remain relatively small and stable. What we're talking about is a Project Brain or Institutional Design Record that preserves the reasoning behind the Estate.

I also think we should build a recovery process.

Rather than dumping one enormous summary, I'd organize it into volumes, for example:

Volume 1 — Vision and Philosophy

Volume 2 — Institutional Structure

Volume 3 — Residents and Offices

Volume 4 — Technical Architecture

Volume 5 — Discovery and Audit Evolution

Volume 6 — AI Infrastructure

Volume 7 — Historical Timeline

Volume 8 — Open Questions and Deferred Ideas

Each volume would be traceable back to the conversations that established it.

About repasting the conversation

If you decide to do that, I think we can do it in a disciplined way.

Instead of trying to summarize from memory, we'll treat the conversation as primary source material. We'll extract facts, decisions, and rationale, assign confidence and provenance where appropriate, and build the Estate's institutional knowledge from that source. That approach fits perfectly with the principles we've been establishing.

I actually think this is the right time to make that investment. The Estate has reached the point where preserving its own design history is becoming just as important as writing new code. That will give Alfred—and any future resident—a reliable institutional memory to build on rather than relying on the limits of a single conversation.

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

Because we're entering a new phase.

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

Edit

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

I'd call it something like:

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

The goal would be to recover everything we've already designed before adding more.

That includes:

Resident biographies.

Office charters.

Personality profiles.

Speech style.

Catchphrases.

Authority boundaries.

Security clearances.

Decision authority.

Relationships between residents.

Trust model.

Architectural decisions.

Why decisions were made, not just what was built.

This is different from the Constitution. The Constitution should remain relatively small and stable. What we're talking about is a Project Brain or Institutional Design Record that preserves the reasoning behind the Estate.

I also think we should build a recovery process.

Rather than dumping one enormous summary, I'd organize it into volumes, for example:

Volume 1 — Vision and Philosophy

Volume 2 — Institutional Structure

Volume 3 — Residents and Offices

Volume 4 — Technical Architecture

Volume 5 — Discovery and Audit Evolution

Volume 6 — AI Infrastructure

Volume 7 — Historical Timeline

Volume 8 — Open Questions and Deferred Ideas

Each volume would be traceable back to the conversations that established it.

About repasting the conversation

If you decide to do that, I think we can do it in a disciplined way.

Instead of trying to summarize from memory, we'll treat the conversation as primary source material. We'll extract facts, decisions, and rationale, assign confidence and provenance where appropriate, and build the Estate's institutional knowledge from that source. That approach fits perfectly with the principles we've been establishing.

I actually think this is the right time to make that investment. The Estate has reached the point where preserving its own design history is becoming just as important as writing new code. That will give Alfred—and any future resident—a reliable institutional memory to build on rather than relying on the limits of a single conversation.

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

Edit

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

I'd call it something like:

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

The goal would be to recover everything we've already designed before adding more.

That includes:

Resident biographies.

Office charters.

Personality profiles.

Speech style.

Catchphrases.

Authority boundaries.

Security clearances.

Decision authority.

Relationships between residents.

Trust model.

Architectural decisions.

Why decisions were made, not just what was built.

This is different from the Constitution. The Constitution should remain relatively small and stable. What we're talking about is a Project Brain or Institutional Design Record that preserves the reasoning behind the Estate.

I also think we should build a recovery process.

Rather than dumping one enormous summary, I'd organize it into volumes, for example:

Volume 1 — Vision and Philosophy

Volume 2 — Institutional Structure

Volume 3 — Residents and Offices

Volume 4 — Technical Architecture

Volume 5 — Discovery and Audit Evolution

Volume 6 — AI Infrastructure

Volume 7 — Historical Timeline

Volume 8 — Open Questions and Deferred Ideas

Each volume would be traceable back to the conversations that established it.

About repasting the conversation

If you decide to do that, I think we can do it in a disciplined way.

Instead of trying to summarize from memory, we'll treat the conversation as primary source material. We'll extract facts, decisions, and rationale, assign confidence and provenance where appropriate, and build the Estate's institutional knowledge from that source. That approach fits perfectly with the principles we've been establishing.

I actually think this is the right time to make that investment. The Estate has reached the point where preserving its own design history is becoming just as important as writing new code. That will give Alfred—and any future resident—a reliable institutional memory to build on rather than relying on the limits of a single conversation.

Edit

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

I'd call it something like:

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

The goal would be to recover everything we've already designed before adding more.

That includes:

Resident biographies.

Office charters.

Personality profiles.

Speech style.

Catchphrases.

Authority boundaries.

Security clearances.

Decision authority.

Relationships between residents.

Trust model.

Architectural decisions.

Why decisions were made, not just what was built.

This is different from the Constitution. The Constitution should remain relatively small and stable. What we're talking about is a Project Brain or Institutional Design Record that preserves the reasoning behind the Estate.

I also think we should build a recovery process.

Rather than dumping one enormous summary, I'd organize it into volumes, for example:

Volume 1 — Vision and Philosophy

Volume 2 — Institutional Structure

Volume 3 — Residents and Offices

Volume 4 — Technical Architecture

Volume 5 — Discovery and Audit Evolution

Volume 6 — AI Infrastructure

Volume 7 — Historical Timeline

Volume 8 — Open Questions and Deferred Ideas

Each volume would be traceable back to the conversations that established it.

About repasting the conversation

If you decide to do that, I think we can do it in a disciplined way.

Instead of trying to summarize from memory, we'll treat the conversation as primary source material. We'll extract facts, decisions, and rationale, assign confidence and provenance where appropriate, and build the Estate's institutional knowledge from that source. That approach fits perfectly with the principles we've been establishing.

I actually think this is the right time to make that investment. The Estate has reached the point where preserving its own design history is becoming just as important as writing new code. That will give Alfred—and any future resident—a reliable institutional memory to build on rather than relying on the limits of a single conversation.

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

I'd call it something like:

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

The goal would be to recover everything we've already designed before adding more.

That includes:

Resident biographies.

Office charters.

Personality profiles.

Speech style.

Catchphrases.

Authority boundaries.

Security clearances.

Decision authority.

Relationships between residents.

Trust model.

Architectural decisions.

Why decisions were made, not just what was built.

This is different from the Constitution. The Constitution should remain relatively small and stable. What we're talking about is a Project Brain or Institutional Design Record that preserves the reasoning behind the Estate.

I also think we should build a recovery process.

Rather than dumping one enormous summary, I'd organize it into volumes, for example:

Volume 1 — Vision and Philosophy

Volume 2 — Institutional Structure

Volume 3 — Residents and Offices

Volume 4 — Technical Architecture

Volume 5 — Discovery and Audit Evolution

Volume 6 — AI Infrastructure

Volume 7 — Historical Timeline

Volume 8 — Open Questions and Deferred Ideas

Each volume would be traceable back to the conversations that established it.

About repasting the conversation

If you decide to do that, I think we can do it in a disciplined way.

Instead of trying to summarize from memory, we'll treat the conversation as primary source material. We'll extract facts, decisions, and rationale, assign confidence and provenance where appropriate, and build the Estate's institutional knowledge from that source. That approach fits perfectly with the principles we've been establishing.

I actually think this is the right time to make that investment. The Estate has reached the point where preserving its own design history is becoming just as important as writing new code. That will give Alfred—and any future resident—a reliable institutional memory to build on rather than relying on the limits of a single conversation.

Edit

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

I'd call it something like:

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

The goal would be to recover everything we've already designed before adding more.

That includes:

Resident biographies.

Office charters.

Personality profiles.

Speech style.

Catchphrases.

Authority boundaries.

Security clearances.

Decision authority.

Relationships between residents.

Trust model.

Architectural decisions.

Why decisions were made, not just what was built.

This is different from the Constitution. The Constitution should remain relatively small and stable. What we're talking about is a Project Brain or Institutional Design Record that preserves the reasoning behind the Estate.

I also think we should build a recovery process.

Rather than dumping one enormous summary, I'd organize it into volumes, for example:

Volume 1 — Vision and Philosophy

Volume 2 — Institutional Structure

Volume 3 — Residents and Offices

Volume 4 — Technical Architecture

Volume 5 — Discovery and Audit Evolution

Volume 6 — AI Infrastructure

Volume 7 — Historical Timeline

Volume 8 — Open Questions and Deferred Ideas

Each volume would be traceable back to the conversations that established it.

About repasting the conversation

If you decide to do that, I think we can do it in a disciplined way.

Instead of trying to summarize from memory, we'll treat the conversation as primary source material. We'll extract facts, decisions, and rationale, assign confidence and provenance where appropriate, and build the Estate's institutional knowledge from that source. That approach fits perfectly with the principles we've been establishing.

I actually think this is the right time to make that investment. The Estate has reached the point where preserving its own design history is becoming just as important as writing new code. That will give Alfred—and any future resident—a reliable institutional memory to build on rather than relying on the limits of a single conversation.

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

I'd call it something like:

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

The goal would be to recover everything we've already designed before adding more.

That includes:

Resident biographies.

Office charters.

Personality profiles.

Speech style.

Catchphrases.

Authority boundaries.

Security clearances.

Decision authority.

Relationships between residents.

Trust model.

Architectural decisions.

Why decisions were made, not just what was built.

This is different from the Constitution. The Constitution should remain relatively small and stable. What we're talking about is a Project Brain or Institutional Design Record that preserves the reasoning behind the Estate.

I also think we should build a recovery process.

Rather than dumping one enormous summary, I'd organize it into volumes, for example:

Volume 1 — Vision and Philosophy

Volume 2 — Institutional Structure

Volume 3 — Residents and Offices

Volume 4 — Technical Architecture

Volume 5 — Discovery and Audit Evolution

Volume 6 — AI Infrastructure

Volume 7 — Historical Timeline

Each volume would be traceable back to the conversations that established it.

If you decide to do that, I think we can do it in a disciplined way.

Instead of trying to summarize from memory, we'll treat the conversation as primary source material. We'll extract facts, decisions, and rationale, assign confidence and provenance where appropriate, and build the Estate's institutional knowledge from that source. That approach fits perfectly with the principles we've been establishing.

I actually think this is the right time to make that investment. The Estate has reached the point where preserving its own design history is becoming just as important as writing new code. That will give Alfred—and any future resident—a reliable institutional memory to build on rather than relying on the limits of a single conversation.

Edit

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

I'd call it something like:

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

The goal would be to recover everything we've already designed before adding more.

That includes:

Resident biographies.

Office charters.

Personality profiles.

Speech style.

Catchphrases.

Authority boundaries.

Security clearances.

Decision authority.

Relationships between residents.

Trust model.

Architectural decisions.

Why decisions were made, not just what was built.

This is different from the Constitution. The Constitution should remain relatively small and stable. What we're talking about is a Project Brain or Institutional Design Record that preserves the reasoning behind the Estate.

I also think we should build a recovery process.

Rather than dumping one enormous summary, I'd organize it into volumes, for example:

Volume 1 — Vision and Philosophy

Volume 2 — Institutional Structure

Volume 3 — Residents and Offices

Volume 4 — Technical Architecture

Volume 5 — Discovery and Audit Evolution

Volume 6 — AI Infrastructure

Volume 7 — Historical Timeline

Volume 8 — Open Questions and Deferred Ideas

Each volume would be traceable back to the conversations that established it.

If you decide to do that, I think we can do it in a disciplined way.

Instead of trying to summarize from memory, we'll treat the conversation as primary source material. We'll extract facts, decisions, and rationale, assign confidence and provenance where appropriate, and build the Estate's institutional knowledge from that source. That approach fits perfectly with the principles we've been establishing.

I actually think this is the right time to make that investment. The Estate has reached the point where preserving its own design history is becoming just as important as writing new code. That will give Alfred—and any future resident—a reliable institutional memory to build on rather than relying on the limits of a single conversation.

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

Because we're entering a new phase.

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

Decision authority.

Architectural decisions.

Why decisions were made, not just what was built.

Volume 1 — Vision and Philosophy

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.

So I think the right move is exactly what you're proposing.

I would stop feature development.

Not because we're blocked.

Because we're entering a new phase.

Estate Knowledge Consolidation

Architectural decisions.

Resident → Service → Capability → Resource

Administration Service
  calls: Ledger Service
  calls: Registry Service
  calls: Capability Service

Capability Service
  knows:
    Kokoro TTS
    F5-TTS
    Whisper
    ComfyUI
    RTX 4090

I don't think you're wrong. In fact, I think you've identified the exact point where a project outgrows "conversation memory" and starts needing its own institutional memory.

There are really three different kinds of memory in play now:

The Constitution — timeless governing principles.

The Estate repository — operational code, registries, standards, assets, observations.

Conversation history — all the design rationale, discussions, personality decisions, ideas that led to the current state.

The third category is where we're starting to lose fidelity.

For example, I remember the broad direction:

Alfred isn't just an assistant; he is the Estate's chief orchestrator.

Residents are offices first and personalities second.

Offices persist while occupants can evolve.

Different residents have different responsibilities, authority, and trust.

We discussed provenance, lineage, and evidence.

We discussed catchphrases, personality, and how each resident should feel distinct.

We discussed security clearances and the fact that the Steward knows things the Estate does not.

But I cannot honestly claim I still have every detail of those conversations. I don't. Some of them have fallen outside my active context window. If I tried to recreate them from memory, I'd be inventing details, and that would violate one of the Estate's own principles.
